explain: The judgment on partial findings falls under 52(c), the oral findings satisfy 52(a)(1), and Reed's motion is timely under 52(b). 52(a)(3) answers his complaint about the Rule 12(b)(6) ruling. 52(a)(2) concerns injunctions, and 52(a)(6) is a standard of review that no court has yet applied.

cites.quote: The court must give priority to actions entitled to priority by a federal statute.

stem: A federal statute entitles Ellis's action to priority on the court's trial calendar. The court's local rule schedules trials in the order the actions were filed, and the clerk tells Ellis that trial priority is entirely within the court's discretion. Ellis asks for priority based on the statute.
ask: Must the court give Ellis's action priority?

options.t: Yes; the court must give priority to actions entitled to priority by a federal statute.
options.why: Correct. Rule 40 says so in mandatory terms.

options.t: No; Rule 40 leaves every scheduling priority to the court's local rule.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 40 has the court provide for scheduling by rule but requires priority for statutorily entitled actions.

options.t: Yes, but only if Ellis has demanded a jury.
options.why: Invents a condition. Rule 40 ties priority to the statute.

options.t: No; priority applies only to actions filed before the court's other cases.
options.why: Invents a filing-order rule. Rule 40 turns on the federal statute.

explain: Rule 40 directs each court to provide by rule for scheduling trials, but adds that the court must give priority to actions entitled to priority by a federal statute. Ellis's action is such an action, so the local first-filed ordering yields to the statutory priority.

cites.quote: When a motion relies on facts outside the record, the court may hear the matter on affidavits or may hear it wholly or partly on oral testimony or on depositions.

stem: Moss sues Birch Co. Birch moves to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction and relies on facts outside the record about where its employees work. Moss disputes those facts. The judge wants to resolve the motion without conducting a full trial.
ask: How may the judge receive the facts outside the record?

options.t: Only through live testimony in open court.
options.why: Wrong. 43(a) governs testimony at trial; 43(c) governs motions.

options.t: Only by affidavits, because testimony and depositions are not allowed on motions.
options.why: Wrong. 43(c) lists affidavits, oral testimony and depositions.

options.t: By affidavits, or wholly or partly by oral testimony or by depositions.
options.why: Correct. A motion relying on facts outside the record may be heard on any of these under 43(c).

options.t: Only if both parties consent to a hearing on the papers.
options.why: Invents a consent requirement. 43(c) contains none.

explain: Rule 43(c) provides that when a motion relies on facts outside the record, the court may hear the matter on affidavits or may hear it wholly or partly on oral testimony or on depositions. No consent is needed, and the open-court rule of 43(a) governs testimony at trial.

cites.quote: A party who intends to raise an issue about a foreign country’s law must give notice by a pleading or other writing.

stem: Vale Corp. intends to argue that French law governs a question in a contract dispute. Vale's counsel gives no written notice of this. At trial she announces orally to the judge, 'French law applies here.' Vale's opponent objects that Vale never gave the notice the rules require.
ask: Has Vale given the notice Rule 44.1 requires?

options.t: Yes; an oral statement to the court at trial suffices.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 44.1 calls for notice by a pleading or other writing.

options.t: No; notice must be given by a motion under Rule 12(b).
options.why: Wrong. Rule 44.1 calls for a pleading or other writing, not a Rule 12(b) motion.

options.t: Yes; notice is required only when the foreign law cannot be found in English.
options.why: Invents an exception. Rule 44.1 requires notice from any party who intends to raise an issue about foreign law.

options.t: No; notice must be given by a pleading or other writing.
options.why: Correct. Rule 44.1 requires written notice, and an oral statement at trial is not a writing.

explain: Rule 44.1 requires a party who intends to raise an issue about a foreign country's law to give notice by a pleading or other writing. Vale's oral announcement at trial is not a writing, so it has not given the required notice.

cites.quote: A formal exception to a ruling or order is unnecessary. When the ruling or order is requested or made, a party need only state the action that it wants the court to take or objects to, along with the grounds for the request or objection.

stem: At trial the judge excludes Rowe's key exhibit. Rowe's counsel says, 'Your Honor, I ask that you admit it because it is a business record, and I object to its exclusion.' The judge rules against her. Counsel does not say the word 'exception.' On appeal, Rowe's opponent argues the objection was lost because no formal exception was taken.
ask: Is the opponent's argument correct?

options.t: Yes; a formal exception is necessary to preserve a ruling for review.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 46 says a formal exception is unnecessary.

options.t: Yes, unless counsel renews the objection after the verdict.
options.why: Invents a renewal requirement. Rule 46 requires none.

options.t: No; a party need only state the action it wants the court to take or objects to, with the grounds, and counsel did so.
options.why: Correct. Counsel stated the action she wanted and her ground (business record), which is all Rule 46 requires.

options.t: No, but only if the objection was made in writing.
options.why: Invents a writing requirement. Rule 46 requires none.

explain: Rule 46 provides that a formal exception is unnecessary; a party need only state the action it wants the court to take or objects to, along with the grounds, when the ruling is requested or made. Rowe's counsel stated both the requested action and the ground.

cites.quote: During trial or deliberation, the court may excuse a juror for good cause.

stem: Midway through a jury trial, one juror's spouse is hospitalized in another state, and the juror asks to be excused. The judge excuses the juror for good cause over the defendant's objection, and the trial continues with the remaining jurors. The defendant argues a juror may be excused only before trial begins.
ask: May the court excuse the juror?

options.t: Yes; during trial or deliberation the court may excuse a juror for good cause.
options.why: Correct. 47(c) authorizes exactly this.

options.t: No; a juror may be excused only before the trial begins.
options.why: Wrong. 47(c) covers excusing a juror during trial or deliberation.

options.t: No; excusing a juror requires the consent of all parties.
options.why: Invents a consent requirement. 47(c) contains none.

options.t: Yes, but only after the jury has begun deliberating.
options.why: Invents a timing limit. 47(c) covers both trial and deliberation.

explain: Rule 47(c) provides that during trial or deliberation the court may excuse a juror for good cause. A spouse's hospitalization fits, and no consent is required. Rule 48(a) then treats the excused juror as not participating in the verdict.

cites.quote: Unless the parties stipulate otherwise, the verdict must be unanimous and must be returned by a jury of at least 6 members.

stem: A civil jury of eight returns a verdict for Park by a vote of seven to one. The parties made no stipulation about the number of jurors who must agree. The defendant moves to set the verdict aside.
ask: Is the verdict valid under Rule 48?

options.t: Yes; a verdict by at least three-fourths of the jurors suffices.
options.why: Invents a supermajority rule. 48(b) requires unanimity absent a stipulation.

options.t: Yes; a simple majority suffices.
options.why: Invents a majority rule. 48(b) requires unanimity absent a stipulation.

options.t: No; a verdict by fewer than twelve jurors is never valid.
options.why: Wrong. 48(a) permits a jury of 6 to 12, and 48(b) permits a verdict by at least 6 members.

options.t: No; unless the parties stipulate otherwise, the verdict must be unanimous.
options.why: Correct. The parties did not stipulate, so a seven-to-one vote does not satisfy 48(b).

explain: Rule 48(b) requires a unanimous verdict, returned by a jury of at least 6 members, unless the parties stipulate otherwise. There was no stipulation, so the 7-1 vote is not a valid verdict. Rule 48(c) would let the court direct further deliberation or order a new trial if a poll revealed the lack of unanimity.

cites.quote: A party waives the right to a jury trial on any issue of fact raised by the pleadings or evidence but not submitted to the jury unless, before the jury retires, the party demands its submission to the jury. If the party does not demand submission, the court may make a finding on the issue.

stem: The court requires a special verdict and submits written questions on breach and damages. The defendant's accord-and-satisfaction defense, raised by the pleadings and the evidence, is not submitted to the jury. Defendant's counsel says nothing before the jury retires. After the jury answers the questions, the defendant demands that a jury decide the accord issue.
ask: What is the result?

options.t: The defendant may still demand jury submission, because the issue was raised by the pleadings and the evidence.
options.why: Ignores the timing in 49(a)(3). The demand had to come before the jury retired.

options.t: The defendant waived a jury on that issue, and the court may make a finding on it.
options.why: Correct. A party waives a jury on an issue raised but not submitted unless it demands submission before the jury retires; then the court may find the issue.

options.t: The issue must be tried to a second jury.
options.why: Wrong. 49(a)(3) lets the court make the finding once the right is waived.

options.t: The court must find the issue for the plaintiff.
options.why: Wrong. The court may make a finding; if it makes none, it is considered to have found consistent with its judgment.

explain: Under Rule 49(a)(3), a party waives the right to a jury trial on an issue raised by the pleadings or evidence but not submitted unless, before the jury retires, it demands submission. The defendant said nothing until after the jury retired and answered, so it waived, and the court may make a finding on the accord issue.

cites.quote: a failure to give an instruction, if that party properly requested it and—unless the court rejected the request in a definitive ruling on the record—also properly objected

stem: At the charge conference, Hart Co. submits a written request for a jury instruction on mitigation of damages. The judge states on the record, 'I will not give that instruction,' and the ruling is definitive. Hart's counsel says nothing further and makes no objection after the instructions are given. The jury returns a verdict against Hart, who assigns the failure to give the mitigation instruction as error on appeal.
ask: Is Hart's claim of error preserved under Rule 51(d)(1)(B)?

options.t: No; a party must always object after the instructions are given, even after a definitive ruling.
options.why: Wrong. 51(d)(1)(B) excuses the objection if the court rejected the request in a definitive ruling on the record.

options.t: No; a failure to give an instruction can be assigned only as plain error.
options.why: Wrong. 51(d)(2) is a separate route for unpreserved plain error, not the only route.

options.t: Yes; Hart properly requested the instruction and the court rejected it in a definitive ruling on the record, so no further objection was needed.
options.why: Correct. That is the exception written into 51(d)(1)(B).

options.t: Yes, but only if Hart objected before final jury arguments.
options.why: Invents a timing condition. The exception in 51(d)(1)(B) removes the objection requirement after a definitive ruling.

explain: A party may assign as error a failure to give an instruction if it properly requested it and, unless the court rejected the request in a definitive ruling on the record, also properly objected. The judge's definitive ruling on the record excused Hart from a further objection under Rule 51(d)(1)(B).

cites.quote: The court must decide de novo all objections to findings of fact made or recommended by a master, unless the parties, with the court’s approval, stipulate that:

stem: Because of an exceptional condition, the court appoints a master under Rule 53(a)(1)(B) to hold trial proceedings and recommend findings of fact on issues to be decided without a jury. The master's report recommends findings for Lund. Moor files a timely objection to one finding of fact. The parties have made no stipulation about the standard of review.
ask: How must the court decide Moor's objection to the finding of fact?

options.t: For clear error, because the master heard the witnesses.
options.why: Wrong. Clear-error review applies only if the parties, with the court's approval, so stipulate.

options.t: De novo, because no stipulation provides otherwise.
options.why: Correct. 53(f)(3) requires de novo decision of objections to findings of fact absent an approved stipulation.

options.t: For abuse of discretion, because the master's ruling is entitled to deference.
options.why: Wrong. Abuse of discretion applies to a master's rulings on procedural matters under 53(f)(5), not findings of fact.

options.t: It must adopt the finding, because the master was appointed to hold trial proceedings.
options.why: Wrong. A stipulation of finality applies only to a master appointed under 53(a)(1)(A) or (C), and only if the parties so stipulate with the court's approval.

explain: Rule 53(f)(3) requires the court to decide de novo all objections to a master's findings of fact unless the parties, with the court's approval, stipulate to clear-error review or (for a master appointed under 53(a)(1)(A) or (C)) to finality. There is no stipulation, so Moor's objection is decided de novo.
